newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan contractor failure renews problem loan fears.
newsitem.headline: Japan contractor failure renews problem loan fears.

text.p: The failure of medium-sized contractor Tokai Kogyo Co Ltd has renewed fears over loans extended to the construction sector by banks and cast a shadow over Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd's plan to merge with another bank, analysts said on Monday.
"We are not optimistic about potential problem loans (stemming from loans to the construction sector)," said Shinano Morita, an analyst at Salomon Brothers Asia Ltd.
If Japan's interest rates were to go up, some of those loans would probably become non-performing or restructured loans, she said.
On Friday, Tokai Kogyo filed for court protection from its creditors after abandoning a plan to rebuild its troubled business. It said that its debts totalled 511 billion yen.

Tokai said its business deteriorated after the bursting of Japan's late-1980s "bubble" of inflated asset prices, which resulted in hefty borrowings and soaring interest rate payments amid falling real estate prices.

Several other medium-sized general contractors have problems similar to Tokai Kogyo's, analysts said. Those contractors have a huge amount of unrealised bad assets including loan guarantees, which are likely to total in the trillions of yen, they said.
With many of the companies having put off decisive action on the problem, Japanese banks have not disposed of their loans to the construction sector, they said.

In the wake of Tokai Kogyo's failure, three of its major creditors -- Hokkaido Takushoku, Tokai Bank Ltd and the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan Ltd (LTCB) -- have said that they would write off unrecoverable loans to Tokai in the first half of 1997/98. They all added that the write-offs would not have a major impact on their earnings estimates.
Hokkaido Takushoku estimated a loss of some 30 billion yen, while LTCB and Tokai Bank said loans outstanding to Tokai totalled 27.9 billion yen and 29.2 billion yen, respectively.
However, some analysts said that they were not optimistic about the banks' projections.
In particular, Hokkaido Takushoku may be forced to post losses in 1997/98 against its current forecast of 3.0 billion yen in parent current profit if stock prices fall, they said.
If that happens, a planned merger with Hokkaido Bank Ltd might not come off, they added. The two banks announced a merger plan on April 1.
"Hokkaido Takushoku and Hokkaido Bank planned to announce the details of their merger scheme in late May, but they have not decided yet," said an analyst, who declined to be named.
"Unless they make a final decision on the details in the first half of the current financial year, it might be difficult to merge next April as they had planned," he said.
Meanwhile, analysts at Nomura Securities Co Ltd said that Tokai Kogyo's action would benefit major general contractors which have accelerated their restructuring efforts over the past few years.

The woes of financially weak general contractors will allow financially strong companies such as Taisei Corp, Obayashi Corp, Shimizu Corp and Kajima Corp to grab a bigger slice of the business pie, they said.
